newsitem.title: INDIA: OPINION - UNION BUDGET - Lloyds Securities.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - UNION BUDGET - Lloyds Securities.

text.p: UNION BUDGET 1997/98 - WILL THE EUPHORIA LAST? - An
analysis of the Indian fiscal scenario by brokerage Lloyds' Securities following the 1997/98 budget.
FISCAL SCENARIO:
** Fiscal Management difficult:

In the current FY so far, revised tax receipts have been estimated to be higher, largely on account of petroleum products and cigarettes. In cases of customs duty, it is largely due to petroleum products, aluminium and plastics.
In fact, all the other major customs duty estimates (revised estimate over budgeted) have been lower with products like iron and steel estimated to show a negative 25 percent growth.

However, excise duty collections have moved up, largely on account of cigarettes and petroleum products. Sectors like caustic/soda ash, organic chemicals and iron & steel are expected to collect far lower revenue than was estimated in the budget. This confirms our view on the industrial slowdown.

On the expenditure side, non-implementation of the Fifth Pay Commission and lower interest burden helped reduce the expenditure, as per the revised estimate, by 23.6 billion rupees. This despite the shortfall to the tune of 44 billion rupees in the capital receipts due to the non-starter PSU disinvestment programme.

In FY98, the government is assuming 17.1 percent growth in revenue receipts. With a lower 15.3 percent growth in expenditure, the budget has targeted for a fiscal deficit of 4.5 percent relative to the GDP.

Assuming that the government has targeted inflation (as represented by the GDP deflator) of 7.5-8 percent, then the government should be looking for a growth of about 7 percent next year. The high agricultural production that proped up growth last year, may not be repeated this year. We expect a moderate industrial growth, in line with that seen last year. Thus the target for GDP growth looks tough.
In this regard, even if the FM is able to achieve his target of fiscal deficit of 654.5 billion rupees its proportion to GDP is expected to be higher.
** Growth in revenues difficult:

The customs tariff reduction in the budget will cause a shortfall of 25 billion rupees (other things remaining same). Thus in order to generate customs collections as per the budget, the growth in custom collections should be of the order of 26.5 percent. However, industrial revenues (representing excise collections) have to grow by 13 percent to achieve the targeted excise collections. Similarly, a growth of 20.6 percent is expected in the corporate tax collections.

If one were to consider an average tax rate of 22 percent, as per direct taxes to PBT of over 1,000 companies, based on first half FY97 results, then the tax rate would come down to 18 percent. Thus to meet the corporate tax collection target, the average growth in corporate profitability should be 42 percent.
Further, personal income tax is expected to increase by 18 percent this year.
The imponderables that remain unanswered is the Fifth Pay Commission's recommendations and its impact on the government.

As per reports, the government is expected to be affected to the tune of about 120 billion rupees and the central government in its budget has provided for 42 billion rupees only (excluding provisions in the defence and railway budget).
Further, the government in the past has been unsuccessful in mobilising resources from targeted PSU disinvestment (FY97 target 50 billion rupees, FY96 target 70 billion rupees).
Last year, the gamble of high growth in imports of highly revenue sensitive products paid off and this has helped to prop up the tax revenue. One has to see if this trend can be sustained.

By undertaking such radical changes in the budget, the Finance Minister has embarked on a tightrope walk. To come out of this unscathed, he has to ensure that the balancing pole is evenly weighed down by a high rate of economic growth and a tight rein on expenditure.
** Will the euphoria last?

The market went up sharply on the presentation of the budget. The capitalisation of Index stocks rose by 5.1 percent in the post budget trading session. This escalation was a result of the market friendly nature of the budget.

This is evident from the fact that the budget carried positive announcements, affecting stocks accounting for two thirds of the market capitalisation. The major movers in the markets were BHEL (9.5 percent), Colgate (8 percent), Hindalco (8.4 percent), IPCL (9.1 percent), MTNL (7.8 percent) and SAIL (8.6 percent).

As the euphoria dies down, the economic fundamentals will take charge. In the long term, the positive impact of the budget will be felt by the stocks representing only 33 percent of the market capitalisation.
